title: From a flight-game idea to a playable island courier with Codex
author: Ready-Drummer-2136
selftext:
I am a product designer. I used Codex to build WINDWARD: a little browser game about flying medicine and mail between islands. This is actual gameplay, not an AI-generated video.



The work was iterative: flight and delivery first, then the red biplane, clouds, forests, camera movement and the interface. The useful part was checking the result in the browser and asking for specific fixes. Camera jitter and trees popping in needed that kind of back-and-forth.



Underneath it is TypeScript + Three.js, procedural scenery and raymarched clouds. The current build has 37 passing tests, including a complete first-delivery simulation. That still does not replace playing it.



Free prototype: [https://windward-liart.vercel.app](https://windward-liart.vercel.app)

What tends to break first in your AI-built games: the controls, the camera or the world?

comments.author: BigDeadPixel
comments.body: I think it is great. There seems to be an inverted normal issue on the plane fuselage though which should be an easy fix. Also I think at least making a setting to invert controls on the y-axis would be useful since that is usually how flight controls work. Very cool idea though.

replies.author: Ready-Drummer-2136
replies.body:
Good catch on the fuselage, that's flipped winding on the procedural body and you're right that it's a small fix. I'd missed it because two nearby materials are double sided.

Invert Y is happening. Five people asked in a day, so it goes in as a setting rather than a swap.

replies.author: Ready-Drummer-2136
replies.body: It's free and there's no account, the link is in the post. If you do try it, the first landing is where people usually lose it, curious whether that's you too.

comments.author: GrokiniGPT
comments.body: Could sworn it was called crosswind

replies.author: Ready-Drummer-2136
replies.body: Different game, mine is Windward. Although someone else pointed out that name is taken as well, so you may end up being right by accident.

comments.author: eliptik
comments.body: Looks beautiful! I especially liked the clouds and colors. Did you use Blender or any 3d software to make the assets? And did you intentionally make it pixelated?

replies.author: Ready-Drummer-2136
replies.body:
Thanks. No Blender, no 3d software at all, every model is generated in code with Three.js. The plane and the towns are geometry built at load time.

The pixel texture is deliberate. It hides the fact that procedural geometry has no hand-made detail, and it keeps the whole thing readable at low resolution.

replies.author: Ready-Drummer-2136
replies.body: Going in. Not as a swap though, as a setting, because half the people who tried it want the current way and half want yours.

comments.author: Plenty-Fox-9219
comments.body:
Airspeed doesn't decrease when you turn? I don't think this is as impressive as people who don't know how video games work think it is.

Let me ask a question. How are you applying force to the vehicle?

replies.author: Ready-Drummer-2136
replies.body:
You're right and it's a good catch. Forces are applied per frame in world space: thrust along the body forward axis, drag opposite velocity, lift perpendicular to the wing scaled by airspeed squared and angle of attack, and the horizontal component of lift when banked is what turns the plane. Cargo mass goes into it, so a heavy load genuinely flies worse.

The gap you spotted is that drag is parasitic only, proportional to airspeed squared. There's no induced drag term, so lift is free and a hard bank costs no energy. That's why the speed holds through a turn.

Adding it, with a test that a sustained banked turn at fixed throttle has to lose airspeed. Thanks for asking the specific question instead of just saying it felt off.

replies.author: Plenty-Fox-9219
replies.body:
Those words mean nothing. Your plane is very clearly just being translated at a speed related to, but not equal to, your displayed airspeed. Banks don't "cost energy" that's not why airspeed decreases.

All your AI is going to do now is make the plane lose translation speed when it turns. That's not what happens when a plane is turned.

replies.author: Ready-Drummer-2136
replies.body: Yep, it's going in as an option. You're the fifth person to ask today, which is a clear enough answer.

comments.author: Ball_Analytics
comments.body: to think I know of a YouTuber who made one actually coding and would follow his channel trying to transition into gamedev. Think it's still on [itch.io](http://itch.io) I still watch his game dev videos he definitely has interesting insights.

replies.author: Ready-Drummer-2136
replies.body: Thanks for the link, watched a chunk of it. Doing it by hand teaches you the parts I ended up learning the slow way anyway. The physics still has to be right, and people notice immediately when it isn't, someone in this thread caught a missing drag term from a 20 second clip.
